## Advanced AI Computing and Systems

Lecture I: Processor Evolution — From CPU to GPU

Prof. Kai Chen

<!-- page: 2 -->

## Syllabus and Readings

## Key Question

Why did AI computing move from CPU-centric systems to GPU-centric systems?

## Today's Path

I. [Review] How code runs and completes computation?

2. [Review] What a host machine looks like?

3. [Core] CPU vs GPU microarchitecture.

4. [Concept] Parallel programming models.

5. [Core] Performance model for AI workloads.

Hennessy & Patterson, A New Golden Age for Computer Architecture, CACM 2019

Dally, Keckler & Kirk, Evolution of the Graphics Processing Unit, IEEE Micro 2021

## Transformation Hierarchy of Computing Workflow of Once Computation

When we write

Y = Model (X), what actually happens?

Step 1: Design an algorithm Model to solve a problem, with input data X.

Step 2: A program expresses the algorithm.

Step 3: System software turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task.

Step 4: Operating system schedules computing tasks and deploys them onto hardware for executing.

Step 4: Hardware executes instructions and moves data to get results.

Step 5: Computation is completed and result Y is returned to the application.

<!-- page: 4 -->

## Transformation Hierarchy of Computing Workflow of Once Computation

When we write

Y = Model (X), what actually happens?

Step 1: Design an algorithm Model to solve a problem, with input data X.

Step 2: A program expresses the algorithm.

Step 3: System software turns the program into an executable, parallel, and robust task.

Step 4: Operating system schedules computing tasks and deploys them onto hardware for executing.

Step 4: Hardware executes instructions and moves data to get results.

"Computing" is more than arithmetic, it is a full-stack process from problems to results.

In this course, we study how system software, operating systems, and hardware make computation faster, more efficient, and more scalable.

## A Quick Review of Host Architecture Roles in AI Computing --- CPU Package: the Host Controller

## Main Function: Run the Operating System and System Software

Install Debian / CentOS to manage all devices

E.g., Install file system, acts as the PCIe root, monitors power and temperature, facilitate data flow among devices, etc.

## Deploy system software and launch codes

Users launch python-based frameworks and calls inference / training tasks.

The CPU prepares input data from SSD/DRAM and calls GPU kernels to dispatch complex matrix computation to multiple GPUs.

Many services are deployed on CPUs such as chatbox, coding agents, webs, etc.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1257_526_2565_1416.jpg" alt="Image" width="49%" /></div>

<!-- page: 10 -->

## A Quick Review of Host Architecture Roles in AI Computing --- GPU Package: the Main Computing Power

## Main Function: Provide High-Throughput Computation

Responsible for matrix and tensor operations and return results.

Package high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to maximum computation efficiency.

Typically, a host server holds eight GPUs, limited by power supply and heat dissipation.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1271_553_2564_1414.jpg" alt="Image" width="48%" /></div>

<!-- page: 11 -->

## A Quick Review of Host Architecture Roles in AI Computing --- NIC Package: the Host Scalable Input/Output

## ■ Main Function: Scale Single Computing System for Distributed Computing

Connect many hosts to execute the same task.

E.g., 5D parallelism for AI training (Lecture 9).

■ A training task may involve thousands of servers, requiring a large network with high bandwidth (Lecture 5).

Package network stack to facilitate GPU-Direct-Networking, bypass CPU to avoid the bottleneck.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1269_553_2564_1415.jpg" alt="Image" width="48%" /></div>

## A Quick Review of Host Architecture CUDA Host-Device Execution Model

## Host -> Device -> Network -> Device -> Host

Host Side: CPU

Allocate memory, copy data, launch kernels, synchronization.

## Device Side: GPU

Run many threads to execute kernels.

## Network Side: NIC

Execute collective communication for remote memory access or copy.

// CPU: orchestrates
cudaMemcpyAsync(h_input -> d_buf);
compute_kernel<<...>>>(d_buf);

// Network library: communicates GPU buffers
ncclAllReduce(d_buf, d_buf, ..., stream);

// GPU: continues computation after communication
compute_kernel<<...>>>(d_buf);

cudaStreamSynchronize(stream);

## The Bottom of Computing: Instruction Execution

■ Instruction execution is the last step of computing.

## Workflow

Load:

from RAM to register file



Compute: add, mul among registers

Store: from register file to RAM

## The instruction efficiency decides to maximum computing power and speed

Motivate two types of PU micro-architecture

CPU: optimize latency of a small number of complex threads.

GPU: optimize throughput of a large number of simple threads.

## CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads Five-Stage Instruction Pipeline

Goal: Overlap time of data load/store

Fetch (IF)

Get instructions from instruction memory/cache

Decode (ID)

Resolve opcode and operands

Execute (EX)

ALU, vector unit, load/store unit, tensor core

## CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads Five-Stage Instruction Pipeline

## Perfect Pipeline

One instruction completes per cycle after filling the pipeline.

No bubbles and maximum throughput.

## For N instructions and M stages:

■ Total Cycles = M + N - 1

Average throughput

= N / (M + N - I) instructions per cycle

■ Instruction throughput per second

Frequency * N / (M + N - I)

## CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads Why Pipeline Stalls: Hazards

■ Any condition that causes the pipeline to stall is called a hazard.

Result: Much bubbles and degraded efficiency

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1386_270_2586_439.jpg" alt="Image" width="44%" /></div>


## Various types of hazards

Data Hazard: Stall due to dependencies of some data

Read-after-write (RAW)

Write-after-write (WAW)

Write-after-read (WAR)

■ Control Hazard: Stall due to branch and synchronization

Structural hazard: Stall due to contention on hardware such as memory channel, cache slot, queue, etc.

## CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads Data Hazards

## RAW

## Read After Write: true dependency

One instruction relies on the output from the previous instruction.

Example: AND waits for R0 produced by ADD.

cannot be renamed away

ADD R0, R2, R1 ; R0 ← R2 + R1 AND R1, R0, #2 ; R1 ← R0 & 2

## WAR

## Write After Read: false dependency

A later write may overwrite a register before an earlier instruction finishes reading it.

Example: AND must wait until ADD reads R1.

renaming can remove it

## WAW

## Write After Write: false dependency

Two nearby instructions write to the same architectural register. Example: SUB must wait until ADD finishes writing R0.

renaming can remove it

ADD R0, R2, R1 ; R0 ← R2 + R1 AND R1, R3, #2 ; R1 ← R3 & 2

ADD R0, R2, R1 ; R0 ← R2 + R1

SUB R0, R3, #1 ; R0 ← R3 - 1

## CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads Optimization #3: Out-of-Order (OoO) Execution

Out-of-order execution separates:

Program order: order written by the programmer

Execution order: order chosen by hardware

Commit order: order that updates architectural state

Typically, the compiler would find independent instruction sets to enable OoO execution, reducing the stall time of the instruction pipeline.

At runtime, CPU involves a controller to find independent instructions while some instructions are waiting.

Preempt current pipeline

Issue independent instruction

Restore preempted instruction when it finishes waiting

<!-- page: 26 -->

## CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads Optimization #4: Superscalar

■ Superscalar CPU: tries to execute multiple instructions every cycle.

■ Need a "wide" pipeline



Wide fetch

Wide decode

Multiple execution units

Multiple load/store paths

Wide writeback

Multi-ported register file

## Challenge:

If instruction pipeline can issue N instructions concurrently,

The CPU needs resolve O(N^{2}) dependence complexity.



<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1305_358_2615_1381.jpg" alt="Image" width="49%" /></div>

<!-- page: 27 -->

## CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads Optimization #5: Speculative Execution

■ Prediction for next instructions

Issue risky instructions on the chance of considerable benefits.

## Benefit

Quick completion --- low latency

Keep deep pipeline busy --- high throughput

## Cost

■ Wrong-path work wastes energy and cycles.

Recovery penalty grows with pipeline depth and speculation window.

<!-- page: 28 -->

bne r10, r2, L_bb
xor r10, r10, r10
L_bb:
bne r11, r2, L_xx
xor r11, r11, r11
L_xx:
beq r10, r11, L_exit
...
L_exit:

loop back-edge branch

## CPU: Optimize Latency of a Small Number of Complex Threads Speculative Execution: Branch Prediction

Naïve speculative execution: Static Prediction

The compiler resolves user's codes and find the branches that would not be taken.

Remove corresponding instructions to avoid control hazards.

## Dynamic Branch Prediction

Learn branch behavior autonomously, no compiler analysis or profiling

Adapt to changing branch behavior

## Example: Why branch is predictable

three conditional branches

Each logical thread has its own architectural state.

Execution units, caches, queues, and predictors are shared.

## From CPU to GPU: Parallelism for Huge Computing Power! Multiprocessors

Problem: How do we scale the throughput of a single core?

With many optimizations, a superscalar core achieves its ceiling --- High Frequency; Deep Pipeline; Minimal Hazards.

Answer: Scale the number of superscalar cores with memory hierarchy, scale the number of servers with networking, and design parallelism.

## Memory Hierarchy (Lecture 3)

■ Multiple cores share global memory (Caches and DRAM)

Tightly Coupled Multiprocessors

## Networking (Lecture 4&5)

No shared global memory

Data exchange via networking

Loosely Coupled Multiprocessors

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1233_718_2537_1425.jpg" alt="Image" width="48%" /></div>

<!-- page: 33 -->

## From CPU to GPU: Parallelism for Huge Computing Power! Multiprocessors

## Parallelism: Do multiple jobs concurrently

Job: instructions, operations, tasks

## Data Parallelism

Different pieces of data can be operated in parallel

Vector processing and array processing

## Task Parallelism

Different tasks can be operated in parallel

Multithreading

<!-- page: 34 -->

### From CPU to GPU: Parallelism for Huge Computing Power! Difference of Scaling Cores: Control vs. Compute

## CPU's Goal: Be general to complex tasks

Hazards are easy to occur, forcing CPU microarchitecture to implement much optimizations.

"Control logic" such as branches and dependencies in complex tasks incur many synchronization among cores.

Result: Scale to hundreds of heavy cores.

## GPU's Goal: Be specific to tasks that are easy to parallel

■ Control logic is less, data parallelism is easy.

Example: vector processing.

Result: Scale to 1,000s to 10,000s of light cores.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_116_1123_255_1225.jpg" alt="Image" width="5%" /></div>


10x to 100x of computing power than CPU!

## GPU: Optimize Throughput of a Large Number of Simple Threads Chip Organization

## Hundreds of Streaming Multiprocessors (SM)s

## Each SM consists of:

Processing units, e.g., INT32, FP32, FP64, etc.

Simplified pipelines compared to CPU cores.

Each unit executes specific instructions that are designed to specific computing precision.

## Warp Scheduler

When deploy multiple threads, GPU packages a branch of threads into a warp.

The scheduler decides which warp would run at one time slot, and these threads hard a register file.

When one warp waits, schedule another ready warp.

High-speed shared memory for intra-SM data exchange.

Tensor core: accelerator for matrix operations.

Tensor Memory Accelerator

256 KB L1 Data Cache / Shared Memory

## GPU: Optimize Throughput of a Large Number of Simple Threads Example: Executing Thread Blocks

A thread block is assigned to one SM

Up to 8 blocks to each SM

Fermi SM can take up to 1536 threads

■ Could be 256 * 6 blocks

Or 512 * 3 blocks, etc.

Blocks

## Each block is divided into 32-thread warps

Scheduling by the warp scheduler within a SM.

Single Instruction, Multiple Threads (SIMT) abstraction

Threads in a wrap should execution same codes/instructions.

However, thread is allowed to execute different branches.

## CPU Multicore Programming: pThread Thread Parallelism with Shared Memory Programming Model

■ Break down a complex task into multiple lightweight sub-tasks.

One process contains multiple threads.

Threads share the same virtual address space, global variables and heap objects are shared.

Synchronization is the programmer's responsibility.

<!-- page: 56 -->

## CPU Multicore Programming: pThread Programming with POSIX threads

■ POSIX threads, also known as pThread library.

A standard for Unix-like operating systems.

Linked with C/C++ programs.

Example: parallel reduction with a fork-join pattern.

Partition input into per-thread chunks.

Compute local partial sums independently.

Join workers and reduce partial results.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_144_895_1243_1495.jpg" alt="Image" width="41%" /></div>


size_t chunk = (n + T - 1) / T;
for (int tid = 0; tid < T; ++tid) {
    tasks[tid] = (Task){
        x,
        tid * chunk,
        min(n, (tid + 1) * chunk),
        0.0
    };

    pthread_create(&threads[tid], NULL,
        partial_sum, &tasks[tid]);
}

double total = 0.0;
for (int tid = 0; tid < T; ++tid) {
    pthread_join(threads[tid], NULL);
    total += tasks[tid].partial;
}

void *partial_sum(void *arg) {
    Task *t = (Task *)arg;
    double sum = 0.0;

    for (size_t i = t->begin; i < t->end; ++i)
        sum += t->x[i];

    t->partial = sum;
    return NULL;
}

## CPU Multicore Programming: pThread Race Condition and Critical Section

Example

sum += local_sum;

For each thread

Load sum

Add local_sum

Store sum

If two threads execute concurrently

both may read the old value;

both compute new values;

one write overwrites the other.

Race Conditions: multiple threads access a shared resource and final result depends on timing.

A critical section is code that must be executed by only one thread at a time.

## Race Condition Example

Two threads update a shared variable concurrently

sum += local_sum;

Initial shared sum = 100

Both threads

read the old

value 100 before

either write occurs.

Thread A

Read sum = 100

Add local_sum = 20

Compute 120

Write sum = 120

Thread B

Read sum = 100



Add local_sum = 30

Compute 130

Write sum = 130

Final shared sum = 130 ×

Expected result = 150



Lost update / Race condition

Because the read-modify-write sequence is not protected, one thread's update overwrites the other.

Serialized access to critical section

## CPU Multicore Programming: pThread Barriers and Condition Variables

Barrier: All threads wait until everyone reaches the same point.

Use cases: phase-based algorithms, debugging, iterative solvers, etc.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_126_628_1192_1370.jpg" alt="Image" width="39%" /></div>


No thread executes until all participating threads arrive.

■ Condition variable: A thread sleeps until a condition becomes true.

Use cases: worker pools, event-driven scheduling, etc.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1399_628_2471_1370.jpg" alt="Image" width="40%" /></div>


A sleeping thread wakes only when another thread signals it.

## Performance Models Amdahl's Law: The Serial Fraction Wins

When problem size is fixed, even a small serial fraction caps total speedup

 $$ S(p)=1/\left((1-f)+f/p\right) $$ 

f: parallelizable fraction

l - f: serial fraction

p: number of processors / threads
